A soft cartilage disk acts as a cushion between the bones of the joint, so the joint can move smoothly. The temporomandibular (tem-puh-roe-man-DIB-u-lur) joint, also called TMJ, acts like a sliding hinge. It connects the jawbone to the skull. There is one joint on each side of the jaw. TMJ disorders — a type of temporomandibular disorder or TMD — can cause pain in the jaw joint and in the muscles that control jaw movement. The exact cause of TMJ disorder is often hard to determine. The pain may be due to a mix of factors, including habits such as teeth clenching, gum chewing and nail biting; stress; and painful conditions that occur along with TMJ disorder such as fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis or jaw injury. The habit of teeth clenching or grinding also is known as bruxism. Most of the time, the pain and discomfort related to TMJ disorders lasts for only a limited time. Self-managed home care, physical therapy for the jaw and the use of a mouth guard can be effective in treating symptoms of TMJ disorder. Surgery is usually a last resort after conservative measures have failed. But surgical treatments may help some people with TMJ disorders. TMJ disorders also can cause a clicking sound or grating sensation when you open your mouth or chew. But if there's no pain or limitation of movement related to your jaw clicking, it's likely that you won't need treatment. This content does not have an Arabic version. * Diseases & Conditions TMJ disorders Request an Appointment Print Diagnosis Your healthcare professional will likely discuss your symptoms and study your jaw by: * Listening to and feeling your jaw when you open and close your mouth. * Watching the range of motion in your jaw. * Pressing on areas around your jaw to find sites of pain or discomfort. If your healthcare professional thinks there is an issue, you may need: * Dental X-rays to look at your teeth and jaw. * CT scan to show detailed images of the bones involved in the joint. * MRI to show issues with the joint's disk or surrounding soft tissue. TMJ arthroscopy is sometimes used to diagnose a TMJ disorder. During TMJ arthroscopy, your healthcare professional inserts a small thin tube called a cannula into the joint space. Then a small camera called an arthroscope is inserted to look at the area and help find a diagnosis. TMJ arthroscopy also is sometimes used to treat TMJ disorder. The procedure can help with therapy, such as releasing scar tissue and removing inflammatory soft tissue and byproducts to improve TMJ symptoms and help the jaw move without pain. Care at Mayo Clinic Our caring team of Mayo Clinic experts can help you with your TMJ disorders-related health concerns. Start Here More Information * TMJ disorders care at Mayo Clinic * CT scan * MRI * X-ray Show more related information Treatment Sometimes the symptoms of TMJ disorders may go away without treatment. If your symptoms don't go away, your healthcare professional may recommend treatment options, often more than one to be done at the same time. Medications Along with other treatments that don't involve surgery, these medicine options may ease the pain related to TMJ disorders: * Pain relievers and anti-inflammatories. If pain medicines available without a prescription aren't enough to relieve TMJ pain, your healthcare professional may prescribe stronger pain relievers for a limited time, such as prescription-strength ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin IB, others). * Tricyclic antidepressants. These medicines, such as nortriptyline (Pamelor), are used mostly for depression. But in low doses, they're sometimes used to ease pain, control bruxism and help with sleeplessness. * Muscle relaxants. These medicines are sometimes used for a few days or weeks to ease pain caused by TMJ disorders that muscle spasms create. Therapies Therapies for TMJ disorders that don't involve drugs include: * Self-care. To ease symptoms, apply heat or ice, depending on the type of TMJ symptoms. Avoid teeth clenching, gum chewing and nail biting. Practice good resting jaw posture with the tongue gently rested on the palate, teeth apart and jaw in a relaxed position. * Oral splints or mouth guards. Often, people with jaw pain will benefit from wearing a soft or firm device inserted over their teeth. The reasons why these devices help are not well understood. * Physical therapy. Along with exercises to stretch and strengthen jaw muscles, treatments might include ultrasound and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, also known as TENS. Also, moist heat and stretching are effective in repeated applications throughout the day. * Counseling. Education and counseling can help you learn more about the factors and behaviors that may worsen your pain, so you can change your behavior. Examples include teeth clenching or grinding, leaning on your chin, or biting fingernails. Surgical or other procedures Arthrocentesis Enlarge image Close Arthrocentesis Arthrocentesis With arthrocentesis, tiny openings are inserted into the TMJ so that fluid can be flushed through the joint to remove debris. When other methods don't help, your healthcare professional might suggest procedures such as: * Arthrocentesis. Arthrocentesis (ahr-throe-sen-TEE-sis) is a minimally invasive procedure that involves inserting small needles into the joint so that fluid can flow through the joint to remove debris and inflammatory byproducts. * Injections. In some people, corticosteroid injections into the joint may help. Rarely, injecting botulinum toxin type A (Botox, others) into the jaw muscles used for chewing may ease pain related to TMJ disorders. * TMJ arthroscopy. Sometimes arthroscopic surgery can be as effective for treating various types of TMJ disorders as open-joint surgery. A small thin tube called a cannula is placed into the joint space. Then an arthroscope is inserted, and small surgical instruments are used for surgery. TMJ arthroscopy has fewer risks and complications than open-joint surgery does. But it has some limitations too. * Modified condylotomy. Modified condylotomy (kon-dih-LOT-uh-mee) addresses the TMJ indirectly, with surgery on the mandible but not in the joint itself. It may ease pain and locking. * Open-joint surgery. If your jaw pain does not go away with more-conservative treatments and a structural issue in the joint appears to be causing the pain, your healthcare professional may suggest open-joint surgery to repair or replace the joint. But open-joint surgery involves more risks than other procedures do. Think about this procedure very carefully after discussing the pros and cons with your healthcare professional. If your healthcare professional recommends surgery or other procedures, be sure to talk about the possible benefits and risks. Also, ask about all your options. fetched_contents.text: TMD Back to top Overview Temporomandibular disorders (TMDs) are a group of more than 30 conditions that cause pain and dysfunction in the jaw joint and muscles that control jaw movement. “TMDs” refers to the disorders, and “TMJ” refers only to the temporomandibular joint itself. People have two TMJs; one on each side of the jaw. You can feel them by placing your fingers in front of your ears and opening your mouth. There are three main classes of TMDs: 1. Disorders of the joints, including disc disorders. 2. Disorders of the muscles used for chewing (masticatory muscles). 3. Headaches associated with a TMD. There are several disorders within each class. See diagram below for some examples. Classification of Temporomandibular Disorders (TMDs) with Examples Text Alternative *A person may have one or more of these conditions at the same time. Many TMDs last only a short time and go away on their own. However, in some cases they can become chronic, or long lasting. In addition, TMDs can occur alone or at the same time as other medical conditions such as headaches, back pain, sleep problems, fibromyalgia, and irritable bowel syndrome. A recent study found that about 11-12 million adults in the United States had pain in the region of the temporomandibular joint. Temporomandibular disorders are twice as common in women than in men, especially in women between 35 and 44 years old. Back to top Causes Injury to the jaw or temporomandibular joint can lead to some TMDs, but in most cases, the exact cause is not clear. For many people, symptoms seem to start without obvious reason. Recent research suggests a combination of genes, psychological and life stressors, and how someone perceives pain, may play a part in why a TMD starts and whether it will be long lasting. Because TMDs are more common in women than in men, researchers are exploring whether the differences in TMJ structure and mechanics between females and males may play a role. Research does not support the belief that a bad bite or orthodontic braces cause TMDs. Back to top Symptoms It is important to know that sounds (such as clicking or popping) without pain in the TMJs are common, are considered normal, and don’t need treatment. However, the following symptoms may signal a TMD: * Pain in the chewing muscles and/or jaw joint (most common symptom). * Pain that spreads to the face or neck. * Jaw stiffness. * Limited movement or locking of the jaw. * Painful clicking, popping, or grating in the jaw joint when opening or closing the mouth. * Ringing in the ears, hearing loss, or dizziness. * A change in the way the upper and lower teeth fit together. Back to top Diagnosis There is no widely accepted, standard test available to diagnose TMDs. Because the exact causes and symptoms are not clear, identifying these disorders can be difficult. Your doctor or dentist will note your symptoms and take a detailed medical history. He or she will ask questions about your pain, including its location, when it occurs, what makes it better or worse, and if it stays in one area or spreads to other parts of your body. The doctor or dentist will also ask if you have other pain conditions such as headache or back pain. He or she also will examine your head, neck, face, and jaw for tenderness; jaw clicking or popping; or difficulty with movement. The doctor or dentist might also suggest imaging studies such as an x-ray, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or computed tomography (CT). Pain in the mouth, jaw, or face may or may not be related to TMDs. Your doctor or dentist may have to rule out other conditions before diagnosing a TMD. Back to top Treatment Before receiving treatment for TMDs, you should know: * Sounds without pain in the temporomandibular joints are normal, happen frequently, and do not need treatment. * Signs and symptoms of TMD go away in many people without treatment. * Because evidence is lacking for the majority of TMD treatments, experts strongly recommend staying away from treatments that cause permanent changes to the jaw joints, teeth, or bite; or that involve surgery. Nonsurgical Treatments Because many jaw joint and muscle problems are temporary and do not get worse, simple treatment may be all that is necessary. When you first feel discomfort in your jaw joints or muscles, your doctor or dentist may have you: * Eat soft foods. * Apply heat or cold to the face in combination with exercises to gently stretch and strengthen the jaw muscles. * Take over-the-counter medications, for example nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), like ibuprofen. * Reduce habits such as jaw clenching, gum chewing, or nail biting. If these steps do not help, or if in the process of trying them your doctor/dentist diagnoses a specific type of TMD, one or more of the following treatments may be recommended. Physical Therapy The goal of physical therapy is to maintain, improve, or bring back movement and physical function. There are several types of physical therapy. One type is manual therapy, in which a therapist uses his/her hands to stretch the soft tissues and muscles around the joint. Manual therapy has been shown to help improve function and relieve pain. Likely diagnosis and what the symptoms mean

The evidence suggests that jaw clicking with pain during chewing is among the most common signs of a temporomandibular disorder (TMD), but it can also occur with other jaw or bite-related problems. Mayo Clinic says TMJ disorders can cause a “clicking sound or grating sensation when you open your mouth or chew,” and that pain is a key symptom when the condition is active [N1-R1]. NIDCR likewise states that pain in the chewing muscles and/or jaw joint is the “most common symptom” of TMD, along with pain spreading to the face or neck, jaw stiffness, limited movement, or locking of the jaw [N2-R2]. Cleveland Clinic adds that TMD can cause “jaw pain, headaches and trouble chewing” and is “common and treatable” [N2-R1]. So jaw clicking with pain during chewing is a strong red flag for TMD, but it is not by itself sufficient to prove a specific diagnosis.

Other possible causes include muscle tension, disc displacement, teeth grinding, stress, or early arthritis, as noted in a health resource discussing constant jaw pain with a clicking TMJ [N2-R3]. This means the clicking may reflect joint dysfunction rather than a purely structural issue, and it may be accompanied by muscle-related symptoms. The evidence also highlights that TMD is a broad category encompassing more than 30 conditions, including disorders of the joint, disorders of the chewing muscles, and headaches associated with TMD [N5-F3]. Therefore, the clicking can be part of a larger pattern of jaw joint or muscle dysfunction, rather than a single isolated problem.

The evidence also helps distinguish TMJ from other jaw or bite-related problems. Mayo Clinic emphasizes that clicking without pain or limitation of movement is likely not a cause for concern and may not require treatment [N1-R1]. In contrast, pain, limited movement, locking, or spreading pain are more suggestive of a true disorder rather than a simple habit or temporary issue [N2-R2]. Cleveland Clinic similarly states that painful clicking can be part of TMD, while NIDCR notes that TMD is a group of conditions affecting the jaw joint and muscles, not just a single cause [N2-R1][N2-R2]. So a key distinction is whether the clicking is accompanied by pain, stiffness, limited movement, or other systemic symptoms, versus being isolated and painless.

On whether the symptoms are typically temporary or persistent, the evidence is mixed but cautiously reassuring. NIDCR says many TMDs last only a short time and can go away on their own, while some become chronic or long lasting [N5-R2]. Cleveland Clinic notes that TMD can be common and treatable with therapies that ease pain and improve jaw function [N2-R1]. Mayo Clinic likewise says that symptoms may last only a limited time and that self-care, physical therapy, and mouth guards can be effective, with surgery usually a last resort [N1-F1]. So the most realistic conclusion is that jaw clicking with pain can be temporary in many people, but it can also persist or become chronic if the underlying issue is not addressed. The patient should not assume it will automatically go away on its own without a proper evaluation.

Overall, the symptoms are consistent with TMD or a related jaw/muscle disorder, but they can also reflect muscle tension, disc displacement, teeth grinding, stress, or early arthritis [N2-R3]. The strongest indicator of a meaningful problem is the presence of pain during chewing, stiffness, limited movement, or locking, rather than isolated clicking alone [N2-R2][N1-R1]. The evidence also supports the idea that some people recover on their own, while others need ongoing management [N5-R2][N1-F1].

What to expect if the patient sees a dentist or specialist

If the patient sees a dentist or specialist, the likely exam will be focused on the jaw joint, muscles, and bite alignment. NIDCR says the doctor or dentist will note the patient’s symptoms and take a detailed medical history, including questions about the pain’s location, timing, what makes it better or worse, and whether it spreads to other parts of the body [N4-R2]. Mayo Clinic adds that the provider will listen to and feel the jaw when it opens and closes, watch the range of motion, and press around the jaw to find sites of pain or discomfort [N4-F2]. Beautiful Dentistry describes a dental examination that includes checking for poor bite alignment, feeling the joint and connecting muscles for tenderness, and pressing around the head for areas that may be tender [N4-R3]. Cleveland Clinic similarly reports that tests include seeing how wide the patient can open the mouth, pressing around the jaw to check for tenderness, and feeling the joints as the patient opens and closes the mouth [N4-R4]. So the exam is likely to be a combination of history-taking, observation, and direct palpation of the jaw and surrounding areas.

Diagnostic tests or imaging may be used if the provider suspects a structural issue. Mayo Clinic says that imaging may include dental X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs, with MRI being useful for issues with the joint’s disk or surrounding soft tissue [N4-F2]. NIDCR notes that imaging studies such as x-ray, MRI, or CT may be used and that a doctor or dentist may have to rule out other conditions before diagnosing a TMD [N5-F3]. Cleveland Clinic similarly lists tests that are used and mentions that the provider may ask how wide the patient can open the mouth, press around the jaw, and feel the joints during movement [N4-R4]. So imaging is not routine unless the provider suspects a specific structural problem, but it is a reasonable next step when pain, stiffness, limited movement, or locking is present [N4-F2][N5-F3].

Likely treatment options depend on the diagnosis and severity. Mayo Clinic says that sometimes symptoms may go away without treatment, but if they don’t, treatment options may include medications, physical therapy, oral splints or mouth guards, counseling, and in some cases surgery or minimally invasive procedures such as arthrocentesis, injections, arthroscopy, modified condylotomy, or open-joint surgery [N4-F2]. NIDCR states that nonsurgical treatments may include eating soft foods, applying heat or cold, exercising, taking NSAIDs, and reducing habits such as jaw clenching, gum chewing, or nail biting [N5-F3]. Cleveland Clinic similarly describes self-care, physical therapy, oral splints, counseling, and other therapies [N2-R1]. The evidence also emphasizes that evidence is lacking for most TMD treatments, so experts strongly recommend avoiding permanent changes to the jaw joints, teeth, or bite, or treatments that involve surgery, unless the evidence clearly supports them [N5-F3]. So the most likely approach is conservative first: self-care, behavior change, physical therapy, splints, and medications, with surgery or more invasive procedures reserved for when conservative treatments fail and there is a clear structural issue [N4-F2][N5-F3].

What a patient can do now without seeing a dentist

Safe self-care measures to try at home include rest, gentle stretching, and reducing aggravating habits. NIDCR recommends eating soft foods, applying heat or cold to the face in combination with exercises to gently stretch and strengthen the jaw muscles, and taking over-the-counter medications such as NSAIDs like ibuprofen [N5-F3]. Colgate similarly suggests relaxing techniques and gentle stretching to help relieve pain, and attempting strengthening exercises once the initial ache has subsided [N3-R4]. Sarh.org notes that “Goldfish exercises” (partial opening) are effective for relieving TMJ pain, while My Centers describes tongue-to-roof stretches, small hinge movements, and relaxed jaw posture exercises [N3-R1][N3-R2]. So the home plan should include a combination of rest, soft foods, heat/cold, gentle stretching, and exercises that improve jaw mobility.

The patient should also avoid certain behaviors or foods that can worsen symptoms. NIDCR explicitly says to reduce habits such as jaw clenching, gum chewing, or nail biting [N5-F3]. The same source also recommends temporarily eating soft or blended foods to let the jaws and surrounding muscles rest [N5-F3]. Colgate and the TMJ Association similarly recommend avoiding hard foods or habits that strain the jaw [N3-R4][N3-R5]. So the evidence supports avoiding clenching, chewing gum, nail biting, and hard foods, while eating soft or blended foods to reduce strain on the jaw.

Warning signs that suggest the patient should not delay care include pain that is constant, severe, or spreading; jaw stiffness or limited movement; locking; or symptoms that feel unusual or concerning [N5-R3]. NIDCR says signs and symptoms may go away without treatment, but it also says that some serious conditions can mimic TMD and that the patient should seek care promptly if symptoms are severe, unusual, or concerning [N5-F3]. Cleveland Clinic notes that jaw popping is not uncommon and typically resolves, but it still recommends waiting at least a week before scheduling an appointment [N5-R5]. The evidence is therefore cautious: the patient can try self-care for a reasonable period, but should not delay care if the symptoms become more severe, persistent, or accompanied by jaw locking, spreading pain, or other red flags [N5-F3][N5-R3][N5-R5].

When to worry and when to seek urgent care

Specific red flags that suggest a serious or urgent problem include jaw locking, displacement, or inability to open/close the mouth normally. Cleveland Clinic says jaw locking may signal a serious underlying issue that needs urgent dental care and warns that ignoring it could result in long-term jaw problems [N6-R3]. HealthDirect states that jaw dislocation is when the lower jaw moves out of its normal position and says to seek medical help as soon as possible [N6-R2]. Cleveland Clinic also says a dislocated jaw is a medical emergency because the person may not be able to eat or speak, and healthcare providers treat it by gently pushing the lower jaw back into place [N6-R1]. So jaw locking or dislocation is a clear red flag for urgent care.

If the jaw feels locked or displaced, the patient should not try to pop it back into place on their own. Cleveland Clinic explicitly warns never to try to pop the jaw back into place on one’s own [N5-R1]. It also says a dislocated jaw is a medical emergency and requires professional treatment [N6-R1]. Bite Align similarly says a TMJ dentist or their assistant may be able to gently release a locked jaw, but the key point is that this should be handled by a trained provider, not attempted at home [N6-R5]. So the patient should seek immediate care if the jaw is locked, displaced, or the person is unable to speak or eat normally.

How long symptoms can reasonably stay before seeing a provider depends on the pattern. NIDCR says many TMDs last only a short time and can go away on their own, while some can become chronic [N5-R2]. Cleveland Clinic recommends waiting at least a week before scheduling an appointment for jaw popping [N5-R5]. However, the evidence also says that if symptoms feel severe, unusual, or concerning, the patient should seek medical care promptly [N5-R3]. So the safest interpretation is: if the symptoms are mild and the patient can eat and speak normally, a short wait is reasonable; but if the symptoms worsen, persist, or include locking, displacement, spreading pain, or severe discomfort, the patient should see a provider sooner rather than later [N5-R2][N5-R5][N5-R3]. In other words, the patient can wait a week if the symptoms are stable and not alarming, but should not delay care if the jaw feels locked, displaced, or the person is unable to function normally.

## Is jaw clicking every time you chew normal?

Short answer: **It can be normal in some ways, but the fact that it hurts and has lasted several months means it’s worth paying attention to.** The evidence points to jaw clicking with pain during chewing as one of the most common signs of a temporomandibular disorder (TMD), but it can also happen with other jaw or bite-related problems [N1-R1][N2-R2]. So if your jaw clicks every time you chew and it hurts, that is not “normal” in the sense of being harmless or likely to go away without any action.

## What could be causing it?

The most likely diagnosis is TMD, but the evidence also says there are other possible causes. NIDCR says pain in the chewing muscles and/or jaw joint is the most common symptom of TMD, along with pain spreading to the face or neck, jaw stiffness, limited movement, or locking of the jaw [N2-R2]. Cleveland Clinic similarly says TMD can cause jaw pain, headaches, and trouble chewing [N2-R1]. So clicking with pain is consistent with TMD.

Other possible causes include muscle tension, disc displacement, teeth grinding, stress, or early arthritis [N2-R3]. That means the clicking may not always be a simple joint issue — it could reflect a combination of joint and muscle problems. The evidence also notes that TMD is a broad category of more than 30 conditions, including disorders of the joint, disorders of the chewing muscles, and headaches associated with TMD [N5-F3]. So the clicking can be part of a larger pattern of jaw joint or muscle dysfunction, rather than a single isolated problem.

## How do I know if it’s TMJ or something else?

The key distinction is whether the clicking is isolated or accompanied by other symptoms. Mayo Clinic says clicking without pain or limitation of movement is likely not a cause for concern and may not need treatment [N1-R1]. In contrast, pain, limited movement, locking, or spreading pain are more suggestive of a true disorder [N2-R2]. NIDCR similarly emphasizes that many TMDs last only a short time and can go away on their own, but some can become chronic or long lasting [N5-R2]. Cleveland Clinic also says that painful clicking can be part of TMD, while NIDCR notes that TMD is a group of conditions affecting the jaw joint and muscles [N2-R1][N2-R2].

So if your jaw clicks every time you chew and it hurts, especially if it has been happening for several months, that is more consistent with TMD than with a harmless habit or temporary issue. However, the evidence does not let you assume for sure that it is TMJ without a professional evaluation [N1-R1][N2-R2].

The evidence is cautiously reassuring, but not overly optimistic. NIDCR says many TMDs last only a short time and can go away on their own, while some can become chronic or long lasting [N5-R2]. Mayo Clinic also says that symptoms may last only a limited time and that self-care, physical therapy, and mouth guards can be effective [N1-F1]. Cleveland Clinic similarly says TMD can be common and treatable with therapies that ease pain and improve jaw function [N2-R1].

So yes, it is possible that your symptoms could resolve on their own, especially if they are mild and the underlying issue is temporary. But the fact that the clicking has lasted several months and is painful means that it is reasonable to worry that it could persist or worsen if left untreated [N5-R2][N1-F1]. That is why the evidence recommends not ignoring symptoms that feel severe, unusual, or concerning, and instead seeking care promptly [N5-R3].

You should also avoid habits and foods that can worsen symptoms. NIDCR explicitly says to reduce habits such as jaw clenching, gum chewing, or nail biting [N5-F3]. The same source also recommends temporarily eating soft or blended foods to let the jaws and surrounding muscles rest [N5-F3]. Colgate and the TMJ Association similarly advise avoiding hard foods or habits that strain the jaw [N3-R4][N3-R5]. So if your jaw is already sensitive, it’s a good idea to minimize chewing gum, nail biting, and hard foods.

So, to answer your question directly: **Yes, jaw clicking with pain can be normal in the sense that it is relatively common and sometimes temporary, but it is not normal if it has lasted several months and is painful.** The evidence supports the idea that it is likely TMD or a related jaw/muscle disorder, but it can also be caused by muscle tension, disc displacement, teeth grinding, stress, or early arthritis [N1-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. You should also avoid habits and foods that can worsen symptoms. NIDCR explicitly says to reduce habits such as jaw clenching, gum chewing, or nail biting [N5-F3]. The same source also recommends temporarily eating soft or blended foods to let the jaws and surrounding muscles rest [N5-F3]. Colgate and the TMJ Association similarly advise avoiding hard foods or habits that strain the jaw [N3-R4][N3-R5]. So if your jaw is already sensitive, it’s a good idea to minimize chewing gum, nail biting, and hard foods.

## What should you watch for before delaying care?

There are clear warning signs that suggest you should not delay seeing a provider. NIDCR says signs and symptoms may go away without treatment, but it also says that some serious conditions can mimic TMD and that you should seek care promptly if symptoms are severe, unusual, or concerning [N5-F3]. Cleveland Clinic adds that jaw locking may signal a serious underlying issue that needs urgent dental care and warns that ignoring it could result in long-term jaw problems [N6-R3]. HealthDirect says jaw dislocation is when the lower jaw moves out of its normal position and that you should seek medical help as soon as possible [N6-R2]. Cleveland Clinic also says a dislocated jaw is a medical emergency because you may not be able to eat or speak, and healthcare providers treat it by gently pushing the lower jaw back into place [N6-R1].

So the main red flags are:
- **Pain that is constant, severe, or spreading** [N5-R3]
- **Jaw stiffness or limited movement** [N5-R3]
- **Locking** [N5-R3][N6-R3]
- **Displacement or inability to open/close the mouth normally** [N6-R2][N6-R1]

If your jaw feels locked or displaced, **do not try to pop it back into place on your own**. Cleveland Clinic explicitly warns against that and says a dislocated jaw is a medical emergency [N5-R1][N6-R1]. Bite Align similarly says a TMJ dentist or their assistant may be able to gently release a locked jaw, but the key point is that this should be handled by a trained provider, not attempted at home [N6-R5].

## What to expect if you see a dentist or specialist

If you see a dentist or specialist, the exam is likely to focus on the jaw joint, muscles, and bite alignment. NIDCR says the doctor or dentist will note your symptoms and take a detailed medical history, including questions about the pain’s location, timing, what makes it better or worse, and whether it spreads to other parts of your body [N4-R2]. Mayo Clinic adds that the provider will listen to and feel the jaw when it opens and closes, watch the range of motion, and press around the jaw to find sites of pain or discomfort [N4-F2]. Beautiful Dentistry describes a dental examination that includes checking for poor bite alignment, feeling the joint and connecting muscles for tenderness, and pressing around the head for areas that may be tender [N4-R3]. Cleveland Clinic similarly reports that tests include seeing how wide you can open your mouth, pressing around the jaw to check for tenderness, and feeling the joints as you open and close your mouth [N4-R4].

If the provider suspects a structural issue, imaging such as dental X-rays, CT scans, and MRIs may be used. Mayo Clinic says MRI is useful for issues with the joint’s disk or surrounding soft tissue, while NIDCR notes that imaging studies such as x-ray, MRI, or CT may be used and that the provider may have to rule out other conditions before diagnosing a TMD [N4-F2][N5-F3]. So imaging is not routine unless there is a specific concern, but it is a reasonable next step when pain, stiffness, limited movement, or locking is present [N4-F2][N5-F3].

Likely treatment options depend on the diagnosis and severity. Mayo Clinic says that sometimes symptoms may go away without treatment, but if they don’t, treatment options may include medications, physical therapy, oral splints or mouth guards, counseling, and in some cases surgery or minimally invasive procedures such as arthrocentesis, injections, arthroscopy, modified condylotomy, or open-joint surgery [N4-F2]. NIDCR recommends nonsurgical treatments such as eating soft foods, applying heat or cold, exercising, taking NSAIDs, and reducing habits such as jaw clenching, gum chewing, or nail biting [N5-F3]. Cleveland Clinic similarly describes self-care, physical therapy, oral splints, counseling, and other therapies [N2-R1]. The evidence also emphasizes that evidence is lacking for most TMD treatments, so experts strongly recommend avoiding permanent changes to the jaw joints, teeth, or bite, or treatments that involve surgery, unless the evidence clearly supports them [N5-F3].

## Bottom line

So, to answer your question directly: **Yes, jaw clicking with pain can be normal in the sense that it is relatively common and sometimes temporary, but it is not normal if it has lasted several months and is painful.** The evidence supports the idea that it is likely TMD or a related jaw/muscle disorder, but it can also be caused by muscle tension, disc displacement, teeth grinding, stress, or early arthritis [N1-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3]. The fact that it hurts and has been happening for several months means it is reasonable to worry that it could persist or worsen if left untreated [N5-R2][N1-F1].

What you should do now:
- Try safe self-care: soft foods, heat/cold, gentle stretching, and jaw exercises [N5-F3][N3-R4][N3-R2]
- Avoid clenching, gum chewing, nail biting, and hard foods [N5-F3][N3-R5]
- Watch for warning signs such as severe pain, spreading pain, locking, or jaw displacement [N5-R3][N6-R2][N6-R1]
- If your jaw feels locked or displaced, do not try to pop it back on your own — seek care immediately [N5-R1][N6-R1]
- If the symptoms persist, worsen, or feel unusual, see a dentist or specialist soon [N5-R3][N5-R5]

In short: you should not ignore it, but you also should not panic. It is a common concern, and many people improve with self-care and professional guidance. The best next step is to try the at-home measures first, and then decide whether you need a professional evaluation based on how your symptoms change.
